newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's disembodied voice greets crowds in parade.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's disembodied voice greets crowds in parade.

text.p: For most of President Bill Clinton's triumphant inaugural parade, the sparse crowds could only see his limousine's dark-tinted windows and hear his disembodied voice calling: "Hello. Thank You. Welcome."

Flush from taking the oath of office on the steps of the Capitol at his second inauguration, Clinton, his wife, Hillary, and daughter, Chelsea, led the traditional parade back to the White House along Pennsylvania Avenue.
But for nearly all the way, no doubt because of security concerns, the Clintons remained inside their armoured Cadillac, its windows resolutely shut.
The president, who loves to work a crowd, used the limousine's sound system to shout out to the spectators as he passed by, calling out simple phrases like: "Hello. Thank You. Welcome."

Although the Clinton family was visible waving through the limousine's gleaming, tinted windows, many people along the route did not appear to be too sure when the Clintons were riding past in the car with USA-1 license plates. Their cheers seemed muted.
The crowds along the avenue, which runs past many of the capitol's historic government buildings, came to life only when an announcer on a loudspeaker told them that the president was approaching.

The Clintons did finally emerge from the car quite near the White House, in an area where the Secret Service appeared to have searched everyone, and walked for few blocks before slipping back into the car and riding inside the White House complex.
During the brief walk the crowds shouted enthusiastically, apparently delighted to get a glimpse of the president and his wife and daughter.

Four steely eyed Secret Service agents walked -- and occasionally jogged -- alongside the specially equipped Cadillac all the way from the Capitol, while dozens of others surrounded the procession, which included Vice President Al Gore and his wife Tipper.
Most people seemed happy to be watching the parade, if somewhat cold.
The one exception was a group of about 30 anti-abortion protestors who shouted "Tell the Truth" as Clinton drove past and held up grisly, graphic posters of aborted foetuses.
After disappearing into the White House for a few minutes, Clinton re-emerged to take his place on an elaborate viewing stand to watch the parade of high school bands and floats.
But the bleachers adjacent to the president's stand were only about half-full and one bleacher, about 100 yards away, was nearly empty, possibly a testament to cold weather.
